name: Science trivia (medium)
description: 38 medium questions about physics, chemistry, biology, astronomy, the human body, inventions. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Who devised the scale of mineral hardness, based on which mineral can scratch another, that is still used today?
items.explain: The German mineralogist Friedrich Mohs devised his ten-mineral scratch-hardness scale in 1812.

items.question: On the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, which mineral sits at 1 as the softest?
items.explain: Mohs chose ten standard minerals in order of hardness, with talc the softest at 1 and diamond the hardest at 10.

items.question: Which of these Mohs-scale minerals, rated 2, can be scratched by a human fingernail?
items.explain: Gypsum has a Mohs hardness of 2, close to that of a fingernail (about 2.2). Calcite, fluorite and quartz are all harder.

items.question: Alexander Fleming shared the 1945 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for penicillin with Ernst Chain and which other scientist?
items.explain: The 1945 prize went jointly to Fleming, Ernst Boris Chain and Howard Walter Florey for the discovery of penicillin and its curative effect.

items.question: The antibiotic penicillin is named after which genus of mold?
items.explain: Fleming realized the mold produced an antibacterial substance and named it penicillin after the Penicillium mold.

items.question: Fleming noticed mold killing bacteria on a contaminated culture plate in 1928. Which bacterium was he growing?
items.explain: In 1928 Fleming saw that a culture plate of Staphylococcus aureus had been contaminated by a fungus that stopped the bacteria growing nearby.

items.question: Which member of the noble-gas group is synthetic and is not found in Earth's atmosphere?
items.explain: All the noble gases except the synthetic oganesson are present in Earth's atmosphere.

items.question: Why were the noble gases missing from Mendeleev's original periodic table?
answers: They had not yet been discovered
He took them to be compounds
items.correct: They had not yet been discovered
items.explain: The noble gases had not been discovered when Mendeleev made his original table. In 1902 he accepted the evidence for them and they were added as a new group.

items.question: In 1868, spectral lines of helium were first observed in which body?
items.explain: Jules Janssen saw distinct spectral lines in the Sun in 1868, which were at first mistaken for sodium. They came from helium.

items.question: Roughly how many bones does a newborn baby have, before many of them fuse?
items.explain: Babies are born with about 270 bones. Many fuse over time, leaving 206 in the typical adult skeleton.

source.title: List of the 206 Bones in Our Body

items.question: Inside most bones, which soft tissue is where blood cells are made?
items.explain: Most bones contain bone marrow, which is where blood cells are made.

items.question: The axial skeleton (skull, vertebral column, ribs and breastbone) contains how many bones in an adult?
items.explain: The adult skeleton's 206 bones split into an 80-bone axial skeleton and a 126-bone appendicular skeleton.

source.title: Divisions of the Skeleton - SEER Training Modules

items.question: The molecule ATP, which mitochondria make most of the cell's supply of, stands for what?
items.explain: ATP is adenosine triphosphate, the universal energy supplier in cells. Mitochondria produce it during cellular respiration.

items.question: Which type of cell, because it needs a lot of energy, can contain thousands of mitochondria?
items.explain: Cells that need a lot of energy, like muscle cells, can contain thousands of mitochondria.

items.question: What kind of weather system is Jupiter's Great Red Spot?
items.explain: The Great Red Spot is an anticyclonic circulation system, a high-pressure centre in Jupiter's southern hemisphere.

items.question: About how long does Jupiter's Great Red Spot take to complete one counterclockwise rotation?
items.explain: The Great Red Spot rotates counterclockwise, completing one turn about every six days.

items.question: The first transistor was invented in 1947 at which research organization?
items.explain: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley made the transistor at Bell Telephone Laboratories in Murray Hill, New Jersey.

source.title: Milestones:Invention of the First Transistor at Bell Telephone Laboratories, Inc., 1947

items.question: Which semiconductor was used in the first working point-contact transistor of 1947?
items.explain: The first working point-contact transistor used a germanium crystal. A working silicon transistor came later, in 1954.

source.title: Milestones:Invention of the First Transistor at Bell Telephone Laboratories, Inc., 1947

items.question: In which year did Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley share the Nobel Prize in Physics for the transistor?
items.explain: The three Bell Labs physicists shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics for their achievement.

items.question: The pH scale is logarithmic. What does a change of one whole pH unit mean for hydrogen ion concentration?
items.explain: Each whole-number step on the pH scale is a tenfold change in hydrogen ion concentration.

source.title: The pH Scale of Common Chemicals

items.question: Which pH value is closest to that of healthy human blood?
items.explain: Blood is slightly alkaline, with a pH of about 7.4. Stomach contents are highly acidic, at pH 1 to 2.

items.question: What is absolute zero, the coldest possible temperature, on the Celsius scale?
items.explain: Absolute zero is 0 K, which equals −273.15 °C. The figure −459.67 is its value on the Fahrenheit scale.

items.question: Besides the Kelvin scale, which temperature scale sets its zero point at absolute zero?
items.explain: The Kelvin and Rankine scales both put their zero points at absolute zero by definition. Rankine uses Fahrenheit-sized degrees.

items.question: At normal atmospheric pressure, water freezes at what temperature on the Kelvin scale?
items.explain: Water at one atmosphere freezes at 273.15 kelvins (0 °C) and boils at 373.15 kelvins (100 °C).

items.question: Scurvy symptoms such as bleeding gums and fragile blood vessels come from vitamin C deficiency weakening which protein?
items.explain: Vitamin C is needed to make collagen. Without it, collagen and the capillaries it supports become weak, which causes scurvy's bleeding and bruising.

items.question: About how long does sunlight take to reach Earth?
items.explain: The Sun is about 93 million miles away, so its light takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us.

items.question: How far away is the Andromeda galaxy, the nearest large galaxy to ours?
items.explain: NASA gives Andromeda's distance as about 2.5 million light-years.

items.question: A parsec, another astronomical distance unit, is equal to roughly how many light-years?
items.explain: One parsec is equal to about 3.26 light-years, or nearly 19 trillion miles.

items.question: In which two fields did Marie Curie win her Nobel Prizes?
items.explain: Curie won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1903 and the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1911.

source.title: Marie Curie - Nuclear Museum - Atomic Heritage Foundation

items.question: In 1898 the Curies announced an element named after Marie's homeland of Poland. Which one?
items.explain: Marie and Pierre Curie named polonium after Poland. They announced it, along with radium, in 1898.

source.title: Marie Curie (1867–1934): Twice Nobel Laureate and Her Enduring Legacy in Radiation Medicine - PMC

items.question: Which uranium-rich mineral did the Curies investigate to isolate polonium and radium?
items.explain: The Curies worked on pitchblende, a uranium-rich mineral, and isolated two new elements from it in 1898.

source.title: Marie Curie (1867–1934): Twice Nobel Laureate and Her Enduring Legacy in Radiation Medicine - PMC

items.question: In May 1952 at King's College London, which chemist and crystallographer captured the X-ray image known as 'Photo 51' of DNA?
items.explain: Rosalind Franklin and her PhD student Ray Gosling captured Photo 51. It supported the double-helix model of DNA.

source.title: Photo 51 and the discovery of DNA's structure

items.question: In which year did Watson and Crick build the first correct model of DNA's double helix?
items.explain: Watson and Crick built the first correct DNA model in 1953, confirmed by the X-ray evidence in Photo 51.

source.title: Photo 51 and the discovery of DNA's structure

items.question: Which gas makes up about 95 percent of the atmosphere of Saturn's moon Titan?
items.explain: Titan's atmosphere is about 95 percent nitrogen and 5 percent methane, with small amounts of other carbon-rich compounds.

items.question: Titan is the second-largest moon in the solar system. Which moon is the only one larger?
items.explain: Only Jupiter's moon Ganymede is larger than Titan, by just 2 percent.

items.question: Which English country doctor developed the world's first successful vaccine, against smallpox, in 1796?
items.explain: Edward Jenner showed in 1796 that infection with mild cowpox gave immunity to smallpox.

items.question: The word 'vaccine' comes from the Latin word vacca, meaning which animal?
items.explain: The term comes from vacca, the Latin word for cow, because smallpox vaccination originated with cowpox.

items.question: In which year was the smallpox virus eradicated, after the spread of vaccination that Jenner began?
items.explain: Jenner's vaccination work led to the eradication of smallpox in 1980.

source.title: Jenner's Legacy: How Edward Jenner's Smallpox Vaccine Changed Public Health
